papers.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can be More Effective than Scaling Parameters for Reasoning
papers.core_contribution: Studies how the effectiveness of test-time inference strategies varies with prompt difficulty and constructs a per-prompt compute-optimal allocation strategy.
papers.methodology: Compares iterative revision and verifier-guided search on MATH, stratifies problems by model-specific difficulty, and chooses test-time strategies within a fixed compute budget.
papers.key_results: The compute-optimal strategy nearly matches or exceeds best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute in reported regimes; a FLOPs-matched smaller-model strategy is compared against a model with 14x more parameters.
papers.key_results_location: ICLR abstract; arXiv §1 paragraphs 8-11 and Fig. 4 discussion
papers.limitations: The practical difficulty estimate still costs inference compute; the study uses capability-specific fine-tuning and MATH, and the hardest questions benefit little from more test-time compute.
papers.math_foundations: Defines a prompt-conditioned compute-optimal policy over test-time strategy hyperparameters under a compute budget.
papers.motivation: The authors frame mixed prior results on test-time scaling as evidence that a single allocation rule hides prompt- and model-dependent regimes.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: available PaLM 2 models lacked revision and verification behavior without task-specific fine-tuning, and the experiment needed a tractable benchmark with automatic correctness.
papers.key_decisions: The paper uses difficulty bins to expose heterogeneity hidden by aggregate curves, best-of-N as the canonical uniform comparator, and FLOPs matching to separate allocation from raw scale.
papers.tried_and_discarded: A PRM800k-trained verifier was ineffective under distribution shift; ORM aggregation underperformed the PRM; lookahead search often underperformed at matched generation cost.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: The chosen difficulty statistic is sufficiently predictive of which test-time strategy works, and the compute accounting makes alternative strategies comparable.
papers.relevance_reason: Closest established conceptual precedent for conditioning a finite inference-action choice on the current instance rather than applying one global policy.

papers.title: Plan and Budget: Effective and Efficient Test-Time Scaling on Reasoning Large Language Models
papers.venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026; accepted, arXiv record)
papers.core_contribution: Formalizes budget allocation across sub-questions and implements adaptive token scheduling after query decomposition.
papers.methodology: A Budget Allocation Model motivates complexity-weighted schedules; Plan-and-Budget compares adaptive scheduling with vanilla and global-budget strategies on reasoning, instruction following, and planning tasks.
papers.key_results: The current arXiv v3 abstract reports up to 70% accuracy gains, 39% token reduction, and 193.8% improvement in the E3 efficiency metric.
papers.limitations: The framework relies on estimated sub-question complexity and heuristic scheduling; its objectives and task domains differ from tool-trajectory security scoring.
papers.math_foundations: Constrained allocation model distributes a query budget across sub-questions according to uncertainty/complexity terms.
papers.motivation: The authors focus on the paired failures of fixed reasoning budgets: overthinking easy subproblems and underthinking hard ones.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: exact uncertainty parameters are unavailable in deployment, motivating lightweight decay schedules rather than solving the theoretical allocation exactly.
papers.key_decisions: The paper decomposes at sub-question granularity, evaluates a joint effectiveness-efficiency metric, and uses global-budget controls to isolate local allocation.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Exact theoretical parameter estimation is acknowledged as infeasible in practice; the implementation substitutes decay schedules.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: The planner's estimated complexity orders sub-questions well enough that nonuniform token allocation improves the accuracy-cost tradeoff.
papers.relevance_reason: A close adaptive-versus-global resource-allocation neighbor that limits ORF's broad novelty claim.

papers.title: Learning When to Plan: Efficiently Allocating Test-Time Compute for LLM Agents
papers.core_contribution: Trains a unified LLM agent to decide dynamically when to spend test-time compute on planning in long-horizon environments.
papers.methodology: A two-stage SFT-plus-RL pipeline primes and refines a planning decision within Crafter and a synthetic graph environment, with fixed-frequency and no-planning controls.
papers.key_results: The tuned 8B dynamic-planning agent reports Crafter reward 0.387 versus 0.379 for a 70B zero-shot baseline while generating 85% fewer tokens; zero-shot planning-frequency experiments use 100 seeds per environment.
papers.key_results_location: Main text §5.3 (adaptive planning efficacy) and Fig. 1 caption
papers.limitations: The authors report that autonomous agents did not fully solve Crafter, evaluation covered specific models and two environments, and planning latency was effectively zero in their turn-based setting.
papers.math_foundations: Planning is framed as a state-dependent advantage-versus-cost decision optimized through task reward and token cost.
papers.motivation: The paper treats always-plan and never-plan policies as two costly extremes and asks whether the planning decision itself can be learned.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: long-horizon RL cost restricted model scale and domains; the turn-based environments avoid real-time planning-latency costs.
papers.key_decisions: It uses a learned gate inside one model rather than a separate router, fixed-frequency policies as distinguishing controls, and SFT priming because RL alone did not reliably induce planning behavior.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Natural-language frequency instructions were unreliable; explicit reward penalties for invalid/long/frequent planning caused agents to stop planning and were removed.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Task reward and token penalties provide enough signal for the unified policy to learn when planning has positive net value.
papers.relevance_reason: Direct agentic evidence that a learnable conditional structure policy can outperform fixed planning patterns, the major capability ORF has not demonstrated.

papers.title: SCALE: Selective Resource Allocation for Overcoming Performance Bottlenecks in Mathematical Test-time Scaling
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 40(40), 34034-34042
papers.core_contribution: Selects different reasoning modes and resource levels for sub-problems based on estimated difficulty rather than allocating resources uniformly.
papers.methodology: Decomposes mathematical problems, assesses sub-problem difficulty, assigns System 1 or System 2 processing, and executes sequentially with context propagation.
papers.key_results: The abstract reports AIME25 accuracy increasing from 57.50% to 71.25% while computational costs fall by 33-53% relative to uniform-scaling baselines.
papers.limitations: The evidence is limited to mathematical reasoning and a different cost/performance objective; it does not evaluate tool-use security trajectories.
papers.math_foundations: Selective allocation follows a difficulty-conditioned dual-process framing.
papers.motivation: The authors identify uniform resource allocation as a bottleneck because hard sub-problems are under-resourced while routine steps consume excess compute.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: the framework must estimate difficulty before allocation, so its gains depend on decomposition and classification quality.
papers.key_decisions: It uses the strongest uniform-scaling baseline, reports both accuracy and cost, and allocates at sub-problem rather than whole-query granularity.
papers.tried_and_discarded: not visible from the authoritative abstract inspected
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Sub-problem difficulty can be estimated reliably enough to select the beneficial processing mode.
papers.relevance_reason: Confirms the broad selective-versus-uniform allocation pattern in another domain, limiting general novelty but not matching ORF's method or metric.

papers.title: Spend Less, Reason Better: Budget-Aware Value Tree Search for LLM Agents
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a training-free tool-agent search tree with step-level residual value estimates and selection that changes with remaining budget.
papers.methodology: Budget-Aware Value Tree Search uses a shared LLM as generator and critic, prunes low-value paths, and shifts from exploration to exploitation as tool/token budget declines.
papers.key_results: Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, the paper reports low-budget BAVT with 5 tool calls at average exact match 0.338 versus 0.334 for a parallel-sampling baseline with 20 calls on OSS-20B.
papers.limitations: The critic adds inference overhead; experiments use one external tool with a uniform discrete cost, leaving asymmetric real-world tool costs open.
papers.math_foundations: Provides a finite-budget terminal-reachability guarantee under stated assumptions and a budget-conditioned node-selection distribution.
papers.motivation: The authors focus on agents wasting scarce tool and token budgets on redundant or dead-end steps that trajectory-level controls cannot interrupt.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: training-free control avoids expensive fine-tuning but relies on the same LLM to provide usable step-level value deltas.
papers.key_decisions: The paper uses matched tool-call budgets, a parallel-sampling control, residual rather than absolute value prediction, and an ablation that separates tree structure, critic, and budget conditioning.
papers.tried_and_discarded: A random tree alone degraded performance; static step-level values improved it but lacked resource-aware control, motivating the final budget-conditioned selector.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: The LLM critic's relative progress estimates are sufficiently calibrated to prune paths before their evaluation overhead erases the budget gain.
papers.relevance_reason: Closest fresh tool-agent neighbor and evidence that ORF's missing learnable, online budget-aware selector is the decisive external gap.
